g.text: Collision handling is the generator's private business, not the service's
All three strategies sit behind next() with no signature difference - which is the only reason the service body reads identically for each.
Interfaces, and what sits behind them
never fails on collision; may block briefly on refill
the ONE coordination boundary, isolated behind one method
hides sharding and replica routing from the service
the hot-key fix is a composition change, not a code change
Refill early, never on exhaustion. A synchronous refill puts a ~5ms etcd
round trip in front of one unlucky create - and does it while holding the
mutex, so every concurrent creator on that instance stalls behind it.
What the only mutex in the design guards
no I/O inside it. This is the ONLY
And what needs no lock at all
Minting across instances disjoint pre-allocated blocks
Claiming a custom alias UNIQUE index on code
Allocating the next block compare-and-swap, retried
Cache writes identical bytes; the row is immutable
Cross-process races belong to the database. Intra-process races belong to a mutex.
Telling them apart is most of what concurrency design is.
resolve(code) - cheapest rejection first, so a scanner never reaches the database
The TTL clamp is what makes read-time expiry correct in the presence of a cache: a flat 1-hour entry on a link expiring in five
minutes would keep serving it for 55 minutes past its expiry. One min() call.
